newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels outline plan for transitional govt.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels outline plan for transitional govt.

text.p: Zaire rebel leader Laurent Kabila outlined his plans for a transitional government on Saturday, saying he refused to work with any political leader who had cooperated with ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Kabila was addressing his first news conference since arriving on Friday in Kisangani, Zaire's third city, which his Alliance for Democratic Forces for the Liberation Congo/Zaire (ADFL) captured a week earlier.
"We say that the ADFL transitional government should be made of ADFL members and only anti-Mobutists and anti-regime people who have never been in power and who never shared power," he said.
A transitional phase would not last more than a year, he added.

Earlier, Kabila and a roaring crowd of 10,000 supporters firmly told U.N. Mohamed Sahnoun there would be no ceasefire with the government before negotiations -- rejecting a plan floated by Mobutu before he returned to Zaire on Friday.
Kabila said he did not see himself as a future president.
"I am the symbol of the resistance of my people against the foreign domination of this country," Kabila said.
"I am not the liberator. I participated in the rebellion, but I don't want to be president. I want my people to be free and then I will return to my private life."
Kabila also said that Kabinda, a town 100 km (60 miles) east of the diamond-capital Mbuji-Mayi, had yet to fall, after earlier telling journalists the town had been taken.
U.N. Special Envoy to the Great Lakes region Sahnoun flew out of Kisangani late on Saturday after brief talks with Kabila.
Sahnoun "understood" why there could be no ceasefire before negotiations after hearing the earlier rally call for the war to continue, Kabila said.
Rebel fighters have seized around a fifth of Zaire since the start of their campaign last October.
Mobutu, who seized power in 1965, returned to Zaire on Friday to shore up his political position in the face of the virtual collapse of his army.
He has spent most of his time in Europe since August, and has had prostate cancer surgery there. He came out of hospital in Monaco on Wednesday.
Mobutu stayed out of the public eye on Saturday, although state television reported that he would resume his normal duties. Supporters predicted he would rest a little first.

The United States and Belgium, meanwhile, sent or prepared to send troops to countries neighbouring Zaire in anticipation of any need to evacuate their nationals. France has already sent troops to Congo and Gabon for the same reason.
South Africa's deputy president, Thabo Mbeki, flies to Kinshasa on Sunday for talks with Mobutu on peace moves.
